# 046 · A lookupswitch bisection rewritten half-open, proved to find every key in a sorted table

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: property holds on every input** | functional, no-false-positive | none | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`LookupSwitch#find`](../../../examples/demo/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/interp/LookupSwitch.java) | [B11: Property proofs](../../../lib/README.md) |

> The interpreter searches the sorted match-offset pairs of a `lookupswitch` by bisection, written the classic way: a closed range, two comparisons per step, three exits. A developer rewrites it in the half-open form, one comparison per step and one equality test at the end. The property committed for the search is its specification: on every strictly sorted table, the result is the index of the key when the key is in the table and -1 exactly when it is not, stated with JML's quantifiers over the array. The prover checks the rewritten bytecode against it on every sorted array up to the bound, and the proof goes through in a few seconds.

## The change

Keep the half-open range `[low, high)` instead of the closed `[low, high]`: `high` starts at `matches.length`, the loop runs while `low < high`, each step compares once and moves `low` past the midpoint or `high` onto it, and the key is tested for equality once, after the loop. The tests for the bisection pass.

**Before** ([`LookupSwitch.java`](../../../examples/demo/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/interp/LookupSwitch.java), line 14):

```java
        return (low + high) >>> 1;
    }

    /** The index of {@code key} in the sorted {@code matches}, or -1 when the default offset applies. */
    public static int find(int[] matches, int key) {
        int low = 0;
        int high = matches.length - 1;
        while (low <= high) {
            int mid = midpoint(low, high);
            int match = matches[mid];
            if (match < key) {
                low = mid + 1;
            } else if (match > key) {
                high = mid - 1;
            } else {
                return mid;
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
        return (low + high) >>> 1;
    }

    /**
     * The index of {@code key} in the sorted {@code matches}, or -1 when the default offset applies. The search
     * keeps the half-open range {@code [low, high)} that may hold the key, one comparison per step, and tests
     * for equality once, at the end.
     */
    public static int find(int[] matches, int key) {
        int low = 0;
        int high = matches.length;
        while (low < high) {
            int mid = midpoint(low, high);
            if (matches[mid] < key) {
                low = mid + 1;
            } else {
                high = mid;
            }
        }
        return low < matches.length && matches[low] == key ? low : -1;
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

The method returns without throwing and `(result == -1 && (\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < matches.length; matches[i] != key)) || (result >= 0 && result < matches.length && matches[result] == key)` holds on every input where `(\forall int i; 0 < i && i < matches.length; matches[i - 1] < matches[i])` holds.

This is a proof over the whole domain (matches: int[] of length ≤ 8 × key: int), not a sample. JBMC turned the statement into a satisfiability problem over the bytecode and showed that it has no solution: no input violates the property.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.mica.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

Binary search is the textbook example of code that is short, obvious and wrong: Bentley found that most professional programmers could not write it correctly in two hours, and the JDK's own `Arrays.binarySearch` carried an overflow for nine years. Rewriting one changes the invariant the loop maintains, and the places where the new invariant breaks are the boundaries: an empty table, a key below the first match or above the last, a table of one or two pairs. Tests cover the tables somebody thought of. A `lookupswitch` that misses a key silently takes the default branch, which is the kind of bug a program masks until a rarely taken `case` is the one that matters.

## Why the verdict is right

The property committed for `find` quantifies over the array, in JML's syntax: assuming `(\forall int i; 0 < i && i < matches.length; matches[i - 1] < matches[i])`, it asserts that either the result is -1 and `(\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < matches.length; matches[i] != key)`, or the result is an index into the table and `matches[result] == key`. The tool compiles each quantifier to a loop in the generated harness, JBMC unwinds the loops, and the array parameter is a symbolic array of every length up to eight with symbolic contents, so the statement proved is the search's full functional correctness on every sorted table of those lengths, for every `int` key. The proof of the rewritten method takes a few seconds. It is bounded in the length of the table, not in its contents or in the key, and the bound is on the page: a reader who wants it larger raises `--max-array-length` and pays in solver time.

## What to do

Merge. The property is the review: a rewrite of a search is accepted because the specification of the search still holds of it, not because the tests still pass. The same property is what refutes the next rewrite that gets a boundary wrong, with the table and the key on which it does.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: JBMC 6.11.0: 5 properties proved over matches: int[] of length ≤ 8 × key: int in 4.3 s; loops unwound 16 times with unwinding assertions.

<details><summary>The statement the prover checked (generated harness)</summary>

```java
/** Generated by jvmcontract: asserts a property of a method on every input. The class file JBMC checks is generated directly; this is the same statement, for readers. */
/* \forall and \exists are JML's bounded quantifiers; the class file evaluates each as a loop over its range. */
public final class PropertyHarness {
    public static void check(int[] matches, int key) {
        if (!((\forall int i; 0 < i && i < matches.length; matches[i - 1] < matches[i]))) { return; } // the inputs the property is about
        int result = 0;
        int e = 0;
        try { result = net.terminalvalue.mica.interp.LookupSwitch.find(matches, key); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { e = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { e = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { e = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { e = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { e = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { e = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { e = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { e = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { e = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { e = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { e = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { e = 15; }
        assert e == 0 && ((result == -1 && (\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < matches.length; matches[i] != key)) || (result >= 0 && result < matches.length && matches[result] == key)); // no exception, and the property
    }
}
```

**Provenance:** Constructed from the two standard forms of binary search (Bentley, Programming Pearls, column 4; the half-open form of the JDK's `Arrays.binarySearch`), on the `lookupswitch` of JVMS §6.5.

- [JVMS §6.5, lookupswitch: the match-offset pairs are sorted so that an implementation may search them by bisection](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se21/html/jvms-6.html#jvms-6.5.lookupswitch)
- [JML reference manual: quantified expressions (\forall, \exists)](https://www.cs.ucf.edu/~leavens/JML/jmlrefman/jmlrefman_11.html#SEC147)
